newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FOCUS-Ukraine grain forecast optimistic, experts say.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ukraine grain forecast optimistic, experts say.

text.p: Ukraine, once the breadbasket of Europe and a regular producer of 50-million-tonne grain harvests, was being overly ambitious predicting a 38-million tonne harvest this year, Western experts said on Thursday.
"Lots of luck," one analyst said.
"A rational person would say 35 million tonnes, and more likely ranging from 30 to 35 million tonnes," he added.

Valentyn Tymoshenko, deputy head of the Agriculture Ministry crop department, said Ukraine was aiming to bring its 1997 grain harvest to 38 million tonnes from a 25.4 million tonne harvest in 1996 -- a record-low figure largely blamed on drought.
But the expert, who asked not to be named, said the agriculture sector continued to suffer from shortages of seeds, fertilisers, machinery, and cash.
"The ground is there but the things that make the ground work well aren't there, like fertilisers, seeds and machinery," he said.
Ukraine's fertile black earth, or "chornozem," once supplied a quarter of the former Soviet Union's grain.
But the sector has been struggling from year to year since the economy collapsed with independence in 1991.
President Leonid Kuchma has yet to appoint a new agriculture minister after sacking Anatoly Khorishko last month, citing "serious inadequacies" in his work.
And Mykhailo Zubets, deputy prime minister in charge of agriculture, is rumoured to be away from his post due to illness, experts say.
"The agriculture sector doesn't have any head, arms or legs," the analyst said.
"But what really matters is whether the government is on a serious reform path and is willing to try things for production and income generation," he added.
The ministry planned to sow 6.10 million hectares with early spring grains, above 5.24 million hectares in 1996, and will need to resow about 500,000 of 7.53 million hectares sown to winter crops.

Acting Agriculture Minister Boris Supikhanov told parliament earlier this week that most of the winter wheat crop was doing better than last year and about 90 percent of fields were in good condition.
Stephan von Cramon Taubadel, an agricultural economist with the German Advisory Group on Economic Reforms of Ukraine, said the forecast was slightly higher than those of previous years.
"If nature is nice to them they should have a nice harvest," he said, but added that Ukraine was short of money to buy fuel, seeds, fertilisers and pesticides.
He pointed out that last year cash-strapped Ukraine could only afford 21 kilograms of fertilisers per hectare compared to over 200 kilograms per hectare regularly used in Europe.

Von Cramon Taubadel also said many foreign companies supplying fertilisers, herbicides and pesticides on credit to farmers, might shy away from providing the materials this year after the government slapped an embargo on exports last autumn.
"They might be more leery this year," he said.
The economist said Ukraine should be able to achieve harvests of 50 to 60 million tonnes, a figure last seen in 1990.
